events.reader:
Selected audience: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs.
Situation context (grounded; check applicability): This is an ops/IT-adjacent person at a company where policies and handbooks are written up in Notion or similar docs and employees communicate primarily in Slack; when someone can't find an answer, they ping this person (or the team channel) directly, and this person has been asked to build or is considering building an automated Slack responder that draws on the Handbook, Docs, and Issue Trackers.
events.reader_segment: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs
events.promise: The internal handbook bot you were going to assemble is now something you configure: one agent over your own policy documents, answering in the Slack channel where the questions already land, with no vector store or backend service of your own to run.
events.arc: Single email. It opens on the launch as news framed in the reader's terms (an agent that answers handbook questions in Slack), makes the case for why it matters to them specifically — the answers already exist, the cost is a person finding them again every time, and the usual fix is a stack they would own forever — then narrows the ask to one agent over one set of policy documents.

emails.job: Get an ops/IT generalist to sign up and stand up one agent over one set of policy documents connected to their Slack workspace — a test, not a rollout.
emails.single_idea: orqAgent is now available: you can put one agent over your own handbook documents and have it answering in Slack, without standing up or maintaining a vector store and a backend service of your own.
emails.objection: Nobody here owns internal tooling — who keeps this running after I build it?
must_not_say: No plan limits, credit counts, execution caps or run quotas — the company's published pricing tables disagree with each other on exactly these numbers, and quoting one invites an objection the evidence cannot answer. The $0 starting plan and 'no card required' are the only commercial facts allowed.

No claim about retrieval quality, semantic understanding, paraphrase handling or answer accuracy. Retrieval is keyword scoring over roughly 500-token chunks, not embeddings, and nothing in the material measures how well it performs. Invite the test on their own documents instead.
No security, compliance or certification claims — no SOC 2, no encryption posture, no GDPR line. This reader is not running an IT review yet, and SOC 2 is only in progress.
No uptime or SLA figures. The 99.9% guarantee is contractual only on Enterprise.

No model-count or provider-count boasting (25+ models, 9 providers), and no list of the other channels — WhatsApp, Telegram, email, webhooks. This email is about Slack and their documents; the breadth list turns one argument into six.
Do not raise speed, breadth, feature quality, effort, control, security or proof as comparison axes — the field is ahead of us on all of them and an email that invites the comparison loses on it.

Do not name or characterise n8n, Slack AI, Dust, ChatGPT Team or any competitor, and do not assert that low-code or homegrown builds fail. Describe the work involved in assembling the stack, not an inability.

Do not state that the reader has already built something, abandoned a build, lost weeks to maintenance or has no tooling owner. If the scene is needed, make it conditional — 'if you have been asked to build one'.
No per-seat versus usage pricing argument: seat economics for the incumbents are not established by anything we can cite.
No customer names, logos, quotes, adoption numbers or 'teams like yours' — there is not one in the material, and an invented one is the fastest way to lose a solution_aware reader.
Do not promise an importer, a migration path or a one-click move from an existing assistant; none is documented.
Do not claim the agent replaces the company's wiki, help desk, backend or documentation system.
No hype register: no 'revolutionary', 'game-changing', 'cutting-edge', 'leverage', 'synergy', or the word 'solution'.
Do not claim voice or telephony support; the capability is unsupported.
Do not claim a full SaaS backend replacement; the capability is unsupported.
Do not claim HIPAA compliance; the capability state is unknown.
Do not claim deep domain-specific operational integrations; the capability state is unknown.
Do not claim reusable per-client agent configuration; the capability state is unknown.
Do not make standalone claims about guardrails as a capability.
Do not promise voice or telephony support unless a current licensed source explicitly establishes it.
Do not claim that the agent layer replaces a company's complete backend, product UI, billing, or operational workflow without direct evidence.
Compliance and certification claims are unavailable unless the Evidence Ledger explicitly licenses them.
Do not claim Knowledge base / RAG context; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Agent guardrails; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Reusable per-client agent configuration; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Voice and telephony runtime; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim Full SaaS backend replacement; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim HIPAA compliance; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Deep domain-specific operational integrations; its capability state is unknown.

Retrieval is keyword scoring over roughly 500-token chunks (E56, E57) rather than semantic search, and the free tier caps the knowledge base at five documents (E120), so a question worded unlike the handbook or spread across a large page.
emails.felt_need: The same policy and handbook questions get asked repeatedly in Slack, and the answers are buried in documentation that is difficult to navigate.
emails.status_quo: Team members search Notion by trying random keywords or guessing document titles rather than getting a direct answer.
emails.why_it_fails: The answers already exist; the cost is a person locating them again every time. As the handbook grows past a couple of hundred pages, keyword guesses and remembered page titles stop landing and the answer turns up three sections deep in a page nobody expected — so the effort scales with the size of the documentation, and every new hire restarts it.
emails.mechanism: The agent is attached to Slack by an OAuth install and replies to mentions and channel messages, so it answers where the question is already being asked. Its source is the documents you upload — PDFs, docs or plain text — and the platform retrieves the relevant passages for each query itself, so there is no vector database for you to run alongside it.

events.subject: An agent that answers handbook questions in Slack
events.preview_text: Point it at your own policy documents, install it in one channel, and read what comes back.
events.body:
The same handbook questions come back to Slack every week. The answers are written down already — somebody still has to go and find them.

The usual route is keyword guesses and half-remembered page titles. Past a couple of hundred pages that stops landing, and every new hire starts over.

orqAgent is a no-code platform for building AI agents, and it is now available. You can put one agent over your own handbook documents and have it answer in the channel where the questions already arrive.

Upload PDFs, docs or plain text — the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query, with no vector DB to manage. Slack connects by OAuth install, and the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

If nobody at your company owns internal tooling, that is usually what stops a build like this. There is no backend of yours to host and no retrieval layer to maintain.

> **$0 to start** — 1,500 free credits, no card required.

Point it at one set of policy documents and one channel. Whether the retrieval lands on the way your team words things is a question only your own handbook answers.
events.postscript: Agent setup runs from the console — under two minutes to a first agent.

edits.line: If nobody at your company owns internal tooling, that is usually what stops a build like this. There is no backend of yours to host and no retrieval layer to maintain.
edits.problem: Two of the three cold readers stopped reading exactly here, and all three named it: the sentence presumes the reader's company has no tooling owner, when this reader is the tooling owner — the person who was asked to build the responder. The email tells them something about their own organisation that it cannot know, and gets it backwards, so the second sentence (which is the actual answer to the objection) arrives after they have disengaged.
edits.fix: Drop the conditional diagnosis of their org entirely and lead the paragraph with the maintenance answer itself, addressed to the person who would own the build: what stays theirs to run after the install, and what does not. Keep it to the hosting and retrieval facts already licensed by E11 — no claim about reliability at scale, no assertion about who does or does not own tooling there.

edits.line: Upload PDFs, docs or plain text — the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query, with no vector DB to manage.
edits.problem: The audience's handbook lives in Notion, and the email silently presupposes the source is a set of files. The reader's first question — one-time export or something that stays current? — is left hanging, and one reader stopped reading here because of it. No evidence licenses a live Notion sync, so the gap cannot be closed with a capability.
edits.fix: Keep the upload fact exactly as E11 states it, but frame the ask so the reader knows what they are being invited to do: one exported set of policy documents, for a test, judged on their own questions. Name the scope of the test rather than implying the upload is the permanent ingestion path. Do not promise sync, connectors, importers or freshness.

edits.line: orqAgent is a no-code platform for building AI agents, and it is now available.
edits.problem: This is the sentence that has to land the one idea, and it lands the category instead. Every reader came away with "general-purpose agent builder stretched to this use case" — the brief's idea is the opposite: the handbook bot they were going to assemble is now a configuration. The generic category line also invites the production-reliability doubt two readers raised.
edits.fix: Make the availability sentence say what is now available in this reader's terms — an agent over their own policy documents, answering in their Slack channel — before any category label. The company's own register ("no infrastructure to manage") is available; the category noun is not what earns this reader.

edits.line: Whether the retrieval lands on the way your team words things is a question only your own handbook answers.
edits.problem: The honest hedge is right, but sitting immediately above the CTA it makes the ask read as a bet on an unverified outcome — one reader said so in exactly those words. The last thing before the click raises a doubt and resolves nothing, so the doubt is what the reader carries to the button.
edits.fix: Move the hedge up so it sits with the retrieval description rather than in the closing position, and let the final line before the CTA state what the test costs and what it produces. Do not answer the doubt with an accuracy, citation or quality claim — nothing in the evidence supports one.

edits.line: The usual route is keyword guesses and half-remembered page titles. Past a couple of hundred pages that stops landing, and every new hire starts over.
edits.problem: Two opening paragraphs describe a problem this solution_aware reader lives daily and has already been asked to fix; the restatement delays the product sentence and costs the room the ownership answer needs.

events.body:
orqAgent is now available. You can put one agent over your own policy documents and have it answering in the Slack channel where those questions already land.

The answers are written down. Finding them is keyword guesses and half-remembered page titles — and past a couple of hundred pages that stops landing, so every new hire starts the search over.

Export one set of policy documents — PDFs, docs or plain text — and upload them. The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query. Slack connects by OAuth install, and the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

If the build would be yours to keep running, here is what that comes to afterwards: no vector DB to manage and no backend of yours to host. We run the agent and the retrieval. What stays yours is the documents and the system prompt.

> **$0 to start** — 1,500 free credits, no card required.

Then ask it the five questions your team asks most, and read what comes back. **One document set, one channel** — that is the whole test, and your own handbook is the only thing that settles it.
events.postscript: Creating the agent itself takes under two minutes from the console.
